60 the normalization of intuitionistic type theory, in which normal
61 forms correspond to the checking mode of bidirectional typecheck-
62 ing, and neutral (or atomic) terms correspond to the synthesis
63 mode. This enables a proof of the elegant property that type anno-
64 tations are only necessary at reducible expressions, and that normal
65 forms need no annotations at all. The benefit of the proof-theoretic
66 view is that it gives a simple and easy-to-understand declarative ac-
67 count of where type annotations are necessary, without reference to
68 the details of the typechecking algorithm.
69 While the proof-theoretic account of bidirectional typecheck-
70 ing has been scaled up as far as type refinements and intersection
71 and union types (Pfenning 2008), as yet there has been no com-
72 pletely satisfactory account of how to extend the proof-theoretic
73 approach to handle polymorphism. This is especially vexing, since
74 the ability of bidirectional algorithms to gracefully accommodate
75 polymorphism (even higher-rank polymorphism) has been one of
76 their chief attractions.
77 In this paper, we extend the proof-theoretic account of bidirec-
78 tional typechecking to full higher-rank polymorphism (i.e., pred-
79 icative System F), and consequently show that bidirectional type-
80 checking is not merely sound with respect to the declarative seman-
81 tics, but also that it is complete. Better still, the algorithm we give
82 for doing so is extraordinarily simple.
83 First, as a specification of type checking, we give a declara-

86 paper, since it possesses desirable properties, such as the preserva-

88 assignment version of System F. Furthermore, we can use the bidi-
89 rectional character of our declarative calculus to show a number
90 of refactoring theorems, enabling us to precisely characterize what
91 sorts of substitutions (and reverse substitutions) preserve typability,
92 where type annotations are needed, and when programmers may
93 safely delete type annotations.
94 Then, we give a bidirectional algorithm that always finds corre-

96 show that our algorithm never needs explicit type applications, and
97 that type annotations are only required for polymorphic, reducible
98 expressions—which, in practice, means that only let-bindings of

100 pressions need annotations.
